hints: Look for which event must come absolutely first. Can a T-helper cell bind to a presented antigen before the macrophage has done any phagocytosis?

Remember the golden rule of clonal selection: presentation and binding must happen first, then the selected cell divides by mitosis (clonal expansion), then the clones differentiate into effector cells like T-killers.
walkthrough:
**Start with the macrophage as the presenter**

Think of the macrophage as the messenger. It must first engulf the foreign microbe by phagocytosis, digest it, and display its antigens on its surface. Nothing else can happen until this antigen presentation is ready. So event 1 is first.

**Select the correct T-helper cell**

Next, lots of different T-helper cells pass by. Only the one with the complementary shaped receptor can bind to that presented antigen. This is clonal selection. So event 4 follows event 1.

**Expand then differentiate**

Once selected, that activated T-helper cell divides rapidly by mitosis to make many identical clones. This is clonal expansion, event 3. Then some of those T-lymphocyte clones differentiate into T-killer cells that go and kill infected body cells, event 2. So the full order is 1 to 4 to 3 to 2.

options.A: Incorrect because 4 cannot come before 1. The T-helper cell has nothing to bind to until the macrophage has phagocytosed and presented the antigen.
options.B: Correct. Phagocytosis and presentation (1), then complementary binding (4), then mitotic clonal expansion (3), then differentiation into T-killers (2).
options.C: Incorrect because 3 cannot be first. Clonal expansion by mitosis only happens after a specific T-helper cell has been selected by binding.
options.D: Incorrect because both binding (4) and division (3) are placed before presentation (1), which is impossible as presentation must trigger them.
